Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report , The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.

The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.

“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.

Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.

“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”

Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”

Interpol and the Chinese embassy have been approached for comment.

stories.title: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
stories.summary: Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.

On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people said.

Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board said it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a company executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

Allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

Their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A company “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.

“He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

“He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

“The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions.”

Others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

stories.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
stories.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tariffs are a signature policy of Trump's office

Published 25 November 2026, 00:38 GMT

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of country's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move comes after the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest rate of "up to 40%", followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to.

The economies subjected to the so-called "Section 301" investigations were: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

Section 301 investigations cover the behaviour and policies of foreign governments and whether they unfairly affect US businesses, workers and consumers.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing the policy will boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

But economists have warned import taxes can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers and dampen global trade.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

stories.summary: The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.”

The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice

Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse.

He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. Any one of them could have pulled the trigger.

In Somalia, locals call these “ghost strikes” because the killer remains a phantom. With so many drones dropping bombs , and so many states (as well as non-state groups) operating their own drones, those being bombed may have little idea of who is killing them or precisely why.

Few countries publish data on where they carry out drone strikes, and even this is incomplete. Often, the only clues come from scattered fragments of bomb casings left behind, or what can be deduced from who is operating in the area or might have enemies there.

The phenomenon is a problem in countries far beyond Somalia. Ghost strikes reflect a fundamental shift in the way people conduct warfare. The machinery of war once required presence: soldiers on the ground or in the cockpit, tanks rolling through the streets, barracks and flags and bases. Only a small number of countries had the equipment – long-distance missiles and air forces – required to carry out a remote war, and those were relatively easy to monitor. Because most armies were physically present, there was also a stronger possibility of gathering evidence and holding them to account when it went terribly wrong: civilians massacred or war crimes committed.

Now, as cheap drones proliferate and become more accessible, thousands of civilians are being killed by remote control , at vast distances, sometimes by operators from countries with no boots on the ground at all. In Sudan’s brutal civil war, drones have rapidly overtaken ground troops as the leading cause of civilian death this year . Most often, no party takes responsibility for a strike. Last month, dozens of civilians were killed in strikes in Tigray, where Tigrayan, Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are all using drones – no one has claimed credit for the strikes or deaths.

On the Horn of Africa – which includes Somalia, Ethiopia and Sudan – the problem is playing out at a grand scale , with at least 11 nations or militant groups operating military drones in those three countries. But we are seeing the same thing in multiparty conflicts across the world, including Yemen, Iran, Myanmar and elsewhere.

According to new data from Drone Wars , more than 55 countries are now operating large, armed, predator-style drones, with seven other states due to acquire them soon. Chris Cole, director of Drone Wars, says this number is probably a significant undercount – the dataset doesn’t include the far cheaper one-way kamikaze models that detonate on impact, and there is nothing forcing countries or companies to announce when they have bought or sold drones, so many more could be acquiring them covertly.

Drones have also become stunningly cheap, in warfare terms. A US fighter jet costs between $80m (£66m) and $300m – amounts that once ensured air supremacy was the preserve of rich countries and centralised governments. But low-cost drones manufactured in Turkey and China are transforming the market, and creating a new set of drone superpowers. A Turkish-made medium altitude long endurance (Male) drone, which can conduct long-distance flights, is equipped with infrared cameras, stays airborne for more than 24 hours and carries more than about 130kg or 300lb of explosives, costs between $2m and $5m for each unit.

Since Turkey began introducing cheap predator-style military drones in the mid-2010s, followed by China in the 2020s, they have become new “drone superpowers” transforming the market and equipping dozens of new countries for air wars. Simpler drones, especially the kamikaze units, can now be bought for as little as $200, with hundreds of new drone startups entering the market, driven partly by the demand of the Russia-Ukraine war. The lower entry cost is shifting the balance of power in conflicts, inviting new players into air wars – even non-state actors including terrorist groups, militias and drug cartels are increasingly acquiring armed drones. It is also making it far harder to track who is killing who.

“The more they proliferate, the more state and non-state actors lay their hands on these cheap drones, the more it makes accountability then really, really difficult,” says Abdullahi Halakhe, an expert on security in the Horn of Africa and Great Lakes region. “This is now one of the biggest problems for civilian protection.”

For Mohamed to learn who had killed his family on 21 May, it would require identifying the bomb fragments, tracing them back to the country of manufacture and finding out who had bought them.

First, however, he had to survive.

Mobile reception is limited in the Golis mountains, and he knew the nearest mobile phone mast was 3 miles (5km) away. The only way to find help was to drag himself in that direction.

It was about noon when Abdullahi Omar, a resident in the nearby coastal town of Buruc, received a phone call saying something had happened in the mountains. The call came in from a nomad outside Baxaya who had come across Mohamed, terribly injured, at a river not far from the cave.

Immediately, Omar began organising a team of men to go out and investigate. “We prepared 36 men in town to go out to Baxaya,” he says.

double quotation mark Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.

The group of men trekked about 19 miles, leaving Buruc during afternoon prayers and walking through the night to reach the site of the strike the following morning. Among those who volunteered for the long hike through the mountains was Mohamed Hassan. “When we finally made it to Baxaya we came across the dead family and injured man,” he says. “There were no Daesh [Islamic State] fighters anywhere, only the bodies of women and children.”

The Golis mountains have been the centre of a global war against the Islamic State in Somalia, with the US carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in the region . The UAE has carried out strikes in the area, but does not publish any data on how many. And Turkey and Somalia’s governments are both also using Bayraktar drones for strikes in Somalia, but publish such minimal data that it is difficult to confirm exactly when or where.

Baxaya, where Mohamed and his family were hit, was supposedly designated a “safe zone” by the Puntland regional government – which was confirmed by Somalia’s deputy ambassador to Tanzania, Ashkir Nuur, who represents the constituency.

“The Puntland authorities have not apologised nor compensated the sole survivor. It happened under their jurisdiction but the sole survivor is yet to receive answers,” Nuur says.

Local people say there were no Islamic State fighters nearby, and Male drone systems are equipped with sensitive, infrared camera systems for monitoring targets that should make it easy to distinguish a fighting force from a family with young children and 250 goats. Who, then, carried out the strike?

The men gathered up the pieces of Mohamed’s children, wrapping them in cloth for burial. As they worked, they heard the insect moan of drones above.

“While collecting the body parts of the family members, we could hear loud engines of planes – we couldn’t see them but could hear,” Hassan says. “Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.”

The men worked as quickly as they could. They took a series of photos and videos to document the strike’s aftermath, showing the bodies of Seynab, Fadumo, Aman and Anab, and the strewn bodies of dead goats. Photographs and video of the strike site taken by these first responders and reviewed by the Guardian confirm Mohamed’s description of events, including the catastrophic blast injuries to his wife, her unborn child, their three daughters, and the subsequent explosion that killed hundreds of his goats. The Guardian is not publishing these images due to their graphic nature.

In a video from the scene, one man stands before the four wrapped bodies, after they have been prepared for burial, and says: “The missile massacred the people right here, and as you have been told, these are their bodies. We want the world to watch this and know.”

Among the drying blood and debris, the men found something else: the shattered pieces of two missile casings, lying in the dirt. With no country claiming responsibility for the strike on the family, these dusty chunks of metal would provide the only evidence trail between the family who died, their killers and the booming, multibillion-dollar industry that provided the equipment.

Independent munitions experts Trevor Ball and NR Jenzen-Jones, of Armament Research services, have analysed the images of bomb fragments left at the scene for the Guardian and concluded that they are from a MAM-series munition, manufactured by the Turkish state-owned defence manufacturer Roketsan.

Jenzen-Jones says the “bomb remnants pictured probably evidence a strike by an unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV], mostly likely a Bayraktar TB2”.

The drone is named for its creator – Selçuk Bayraktar, one of the stars of Turkey’s drone industry. His company, Baykar, has had a meteoric rise since it brought the first Bayraktar drone on to the global market in 2014, and works closely with state-owned defence companies, arming its drones with Rokestan munitions. In 2016, Bayraktar married Sümeyye Erdoğan, the daughter of the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in a lavish wedding ceremony, drawing Baykar into even closer connection with its government.

Turkey is a relatively recent entrant to the drone market, but it has rapidly dominated sales to new states buying large, predator-style drones – particularly across African and Arab countries. On the back of its drone manufacturers, the country’s entire defence export market has boomed, reaching more than £7.5bn last year , up more than 500% from a decade earlier . The country now claims to control 65% of the global drone market , and Baykar has become one of the world’s biggest military drone companies. This year, the country’s military exports are tracking toward a new record high.

At the same time, Turkey has developed a reputation for relatively lax “no questions asked” export rules. A large portion of the governments that Turkey has sold drones to in the past five years are classed as fully authoritarian regimes (including Mali, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Rwanda, Turkmenistan, Qatar, Uzbekistan, Chad, Togo, Niger, Tunisia, Djibouti, Burkina Faso, Kuwait, Libya, Somalia) and/or already embroiled in civil war or armed internal conflict (including but not limited to Sudan, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Somalia) . Numerous states on Turkey’s customer list have subsequently been accused of mass killings of civilians using their equipment. For Ankara, however, the explosion of the drone market has been a geopolitical success – with Turkey leveraging drone sales to massively grow its overseas political and military influence.

A Turkish diplomatic representative said: “Turkish UAV exports to Sudan or Somalia, like those to other countries, are subject to guarantees that they will be used in full compliance with international law. There is no verified information indicating that Turkish-manufactured UAVs have been used in violation of the relevant international norms and regulations by the Sudanese Army or in Somalia.”

Even tracing the missile that killed Mohamed’s family to its source, however, does not tell us who was responsible for pulling the trigger. The UAE, Turkey and the Somali government all fly Bayraktar drones in Somali skies. The US has also carried out hundreds of strikes in the region, but using its own drones.

The Turkish, Somali and UAE governments did not respond to requests for comment on who dropped the bomb on Mohamed and his family. Here, the trail runs cold. Seynab, Aman, Anab and Fadumo’s killers remain ghosts.

Hours after they arrived, the men began the long trek back through the mountains toward the coast. Hassan was one of those who carried Mohamed, hauling his body over the difficult, rocky terrain of the mountains for more than 24 hours.

The whole way, the sound of planes followed them.

“It would go away, then once again the noise would return, so we knew our every step was being watched,” Hassan says. “We were scared because we knew what the planes did to Mohamed and his family … They were innocent people, who did nothing wrong and were massacred by these same planes now hovering above us.” From Buruc, the company sent Mohamed on a raft to Bosaso, the nearest equipped hospital, for treatment.

Before Mohamed had even arrived at the hospital, Abdulkadir Koudah, a family member, had heard the news and contacted local security services to inform them that a man who was the sole survivor of an airstrike was on his way. In the months since, “they haven’t helped us or given us any answers on who bombed the family”, he says.

Mohamed is slowly recovering, although the wounds are still visible on his body. Still, he says: “The burns on my body are nothing compared to what my daughters went through.

“They were excited about having another sibling and so was their mother, but everything changed in the blink of an eye and I don’t know who to blame.”

stories.title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel

Published 24 November 2026

Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness", later telling the Commons an interim report would be published by the 75th anniversary of the first test, in October next year.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

BBC Newsnight special on nuclear test veterans

Victoria Derbyshire speaks to veterans as an independent panel is announced into health impacts

Watch now on iPlayer

Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.

Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.

Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.

The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the Labrats (Legacy of the Atomic Bomb: Recognition for Atomic Test Survivors) group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.

Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.

Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers.

He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years.

"Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."

Barbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.

She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."

Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.

He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."

Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.

On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of.

"Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told campaigners in Downing Street that he would launch an independent investigation

Alan Owen, whose father was exposed to radiation while serving with the Royal Navy and died aged 52, told BBC Breakfast that along with the inquiry other measures had also been agreed, including a new education programme about nuclear test veterans and research for descendants who believe their conditions may be linked to the radiation tests.

"It's going to take time, but it needs to be done correctly," he said.

The prime minister told the Commons on Wednesday that an interim report would be followed by final findings "as quickly as possible".

Burnham said further action on education and research will continue while work on the report is being done, including organising a national memorial service for next October, on the 75th anniversary of the first test.

Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was "absolutely right" to talk about justice for veterans, but asked whether the government had made provisions for issuing compensation if necessary.

The prime minister said: "We should go wherever the truth takes us and we should make whatever recompense is needed as a result but those are questions that will come in the next phase."

The MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.

However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026 , though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.

Burnham told MPs medical for the veterans do exist and it was "indefensible" they have been withheld.

'Serious allegations against the state'

The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.

He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."

Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."

He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit.

He said the panel would "help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed".

Asked if the government would pay compensation should the panel recommend it, Streeting said he would not pre-judge its report but that he felt "absolutely sure the findings will be uncomfortable" and the government "will have to take that on the chin".

stories.title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
stories.summary: "Without this funding, activities would be delayed."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“Without this funding, activities would be delayed.”

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government ( PDF ).

The list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”

The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

Another continuing resolution?

Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

Given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the new year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

Flexibility for Isaacman

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission plan that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test issues.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

“Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

stories.body:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures , regulatory proceedings , and the courts . The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976 , which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709 .

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives , meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors , while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users .

What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves , since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies " de-identify " age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives —meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize ) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends , support groups , community organizing , local news , creative audiences , and ways to speak out on current issues . U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information , and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice . Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth , however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Help Us Help You

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate . If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org .

Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

stories.title: Burnham defends inviting influencers into No 10 in PMQs row with Badenoch
stories.summary: The Tory leader calls on the PM to apologise for allowing an "obscene" video to be recorded outside Number 10.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 November 2026, 11:46 GMT

Andy Burnham has defended his use of social media influencers to get the government's message across to young people in angry exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at Prime Minister's Questions.

The Conservative leader called on the prime minister to apologise for "debasing his office" by allowing a content creator to record a video on the steps of Number 10, which included "vile" and "obscene" comments about women.

Burnham said the video had been taken down and its creator had "rightly apologised" for it.

But he said he would not apologise for engaging with influencers who "young people themselves are looking to for their information" and accused Badenoch of "sneering" at TikTokers.

Max Balegde has 3.6m followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram

About 60 content creators were invited to a Downing Street reception last month, with videos from the event, including of Burnham DJing, subsequently emerging online.

In one video, Max Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Badenoch said the words used were "so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House".

"Disgusting and pejorative comments about women's private parts, obscene language that referred to white women as cheap meat.

"This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitment to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday, I won't be."

Burnham said the Tory leader was "right to call out that, because it was not acceptable" but he would "not apologise" for engaging with young people.

"She sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers," he added, accusing Badenoch of "having nothing positive to say to the country" and of "constantly talking it down".

The two leaders continued the argument throughout their weekly Commons clash, with Burnham saying "it's true I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to this House, with the opposite of influencers".

Badenoch said the PM preferred to "take questions to people dancing around Downing Street", a reference to a video of another content creator dancing through Number 10 and down the stairs in an attempt to recreate a scene from the film Love, Actually.

This prompted Burnham to make a jibe about "lockdown parties" in Downing Street during the Covid pandemic.

Responding to the row about his now-deleted TikTok video in an Instagram post on Tuesday, Balegde said: "My content is always meant to be silly, fun, and light-hearted.

"If anybody was offended by that video, I sincerely apologise."

But he said "nobody was offended for weeks until revolting right-wing people tried to put this disgusting narrative on it".

"And if anybody then looks at the video and is offended, I get that. So hence why I took it down because I think that is disgusting."

Sophie Tea, from the West Midlands, now lives and works in London

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

Artist Sophie Tea, who has more than 1.3 million followers on TikTok, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been "excited" to be invited to the Downing Street reception, describing it as a "privilege".

"I believe in the democratization of information and I think this opportunity was perfect for me to be able to understand more what's going on.

"Number 10 is meant to represent the whole country and the more people feel like they belong there, the better."

She said she was looking to use her social media platform to "communicate to the UK some of the brilliant things that are happening in government".

Asked if she was being used by the government, she said "absolutely" but it was "mutually exploitative" because, as an independent artist, she had used it to "prop up my own value".

This isn't the first time influencers have been invited into Downing Street. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was interviewed by content creators during his time in office.

Nor is it the first time they have descended onto Number 10 en masse, with the first content creator reception taking place under Sir Keir Starmer's leadership in 2025.

Content creators are also regularly invited to press conferences and government briefings, including an event at Number 11 Downing Street on the day of the Budget last month.

Writing on X, Luke Tryl, the UK director of pollsters More In Common, said it was "sensible" for Burnham to use influencers to reach a wider audience and it was "helping the PM seem in touch".

But, he added, the PM's "biggest weakness" was being seen as a "people pleaser" and he should also do "non-softball interviews with traditional scrutiny media" to help tackle that.

stories.title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
stories.summary: Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app. Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “ Intelligent Screen Context ,” while Apple refers to it as either “ Onscreen Awareness ” or “ Visual Intelligence .” Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option. While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

stories.summary: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. Our US Politics Live blog is keeping tabs on the latest developments:

The rapid expansion of AI data centre construction could exacerbate the US housing shortage by drawing workers away from homebuilding.

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo , Professor Dame Wendy Hall , Stuart J. Russell and Alexandra Birch-Mayne as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

Book tickets here or at guardian.live

The S&P 500, the flagship US share index, is down 0.4% in early trading at 7,206 points.

Democratic senator Bernie Sanders has warned US tech companies not to expect a bailout if their AI investments turn sour.

WSJ: US prepares to raise tariffs on China and other countries

Fears of a new US-China trade war are rippling through the markets today too.

The Wall Street Journal are reporting that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, according to people familiar with the plans.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could release the results of a tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations later this week, the WSJ adds…..

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene has warned that UK interest rates need to keep rising, unless there is a “miraculous” breakthough in the Middle East conflict.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on their apps – and the high street.

But, Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen points out that there are ‘clear differences’ with the other big risk-off moves of the last decade:

That’s based on the US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

The US dollar, which hit a 19-month high yesterday, has dipped by 0.3% against a basket of currencies.

That weakness is helping the pound – it’s up half a cent at $1.3088, up from a one-year low yesterday.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Published 24 November 2026

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.

With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia Published 13 hours ago

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .

But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 19 hours ago

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, its chairman, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

On Monday, Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .

Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.

Republican Congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners

Newsflash: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, according to reports.

The US Trade Representative’s office announced the duties after completing an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe into 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan , the European Union and South Korea , Reuters reports .

The move is designed to clamp down on ‘structural excess industrial capacity’.

A senior US official said that tariffs were proposed for goods from China , Bangladesh , Cambodia , the European Union , India , Indonesia , Japan , South Korea, Malaysia , Singapore , Switzerland , Taiwan , Thailand and Vietnam .

The specific rates are expected to be published in a US Federal Register notice later today.

The move follows the Supreme Court’s striking down of broader tariffs announced by President Trump.

Associated Press have more details of today’s move:

double quotation mark The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. A senior administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes . Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker. For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

New US tariffs proposed: what the experts say

These new proposed tariffs are ‘the last thing’ the market needs, when investors are already dealing with AI jitters, says Aneeka Gupta , director and equity strategist at Wisdomtree .

double quotation mark “The market is still dealing with the doubts that are being raised on further capex expansion plans by the tech space. And the last thing the market needed was to now see Trump rebuilding the tariff regime once again.” “I think given the fact that the market’s focus really is on the tech ‌space, we aren’t seeing as big of a reaction.”

The big question is whether these tariffs last longer than previous levies which were blocked by the US courts .

Lee Hardman , senior currency analyst at Japanese bank MUFG , explains:

double quotation mark “From ​a market perspective it’s not ​that surprising and I don’t see it ​being a big market mover. The main market focus at the moment is ​on what’s happening in ‌AI-related investments. The Trump ​administration finding an alternative ​way for the tariffs back in place, and as it’s replacing similar tariff rates it shouldn’t have a major effect on the inflation outlook. The next thing to watch is if these tariffs can stand the test of the time.“

US economy grows at fastest pace in three years

The US economy grew at the fastest pace in three years in the quarter to September, while claims for unemployment benefits fell, according to official figures.

GDP rose by an annualised 4.3% in the third quarter, revised up from the 3.4% reported last month, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis . Economists had forecast 3.5% growth.

Investment and consumer spending were stronger than previously thought, while government spending also rose, partly offset by a decline in exports.

Meanwhile, the number of people filing new claims for unemployment benefits in the US fell by 13,000 to 189,000 in the third week of November, well below market expectations of 200,000. It was the joint lowest figure in nearly six decades.

Continuing jobless claims, a gauge of outstanding unemployment, fell by 95,000 to 1,697,000 in the second week of the month, the lowest since 2023. This points to a resilient labour market.

The dollar rose by 0.13% against a basket of major currencies after the data. The pound fell 0.35% to $1.3067.

Stock futures extended losses, as the data bolstered expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December.

The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at an annual rate of 3.8% in October, matching analysts’ forecasts, while the core rate (which strips out volatile food and energy costs) was 3.3%, slightly higher than expected.

double quotation mark The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods.
