For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“Blame obscene profiteering of energy companies, not people who can’t afford to pay their bills”, said Green leader Zack Polanski.

With the price cap announcement today confirming a 26% rise in family energy bills, energy bosses continue to blame the public, he said.

Ahead of the increase, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica said on Sunday that he was “hugely concerned” about the impact on consumers.

Chris O’Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

O’Shea added there was a “massive problem” with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an “increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills”.

He said the collective impact was that “every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it’s just going to get worse when bills go up”.

Polanski said:

double quotation mark As millions of people, including single parents, have to make difficult choices on how to keep their young children warm in our coldest months, the public won’t stand for the hypocrisy of energy companies who put profit for an elite few over people. The Labour government, instead of listening to fossil fuel lobbyists and Donald Trump, needs to crack down on obscene profiteering by energy companies, who should be investing in clean energy, not lecturing and blaming the public who are at breaking point and can’t afford these rip off bills.

Amazon motors into £200bn UK car market

Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market.

The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from Korean manufacturer Hyundai . It will be the first time the US company has sold cars outside its home country.

Amazon, which is the world’s biggest online retailer with a market value of $2.7tn, started selling cars at the end of 2024 in an effort to expand into one of the few remaining major consumer markets it had not already targeted.

Its latest move will be watched closely by car retailers that share a market worth more than £200bn a year.

Amazon Autos operates in 150 US cities and counts thousands of dealers in its networks, offering vehicles from 35 brands.

UK buyers will be able to buy new electric hybrid and petrol Hyundai models, as well as used cars from Vertu Motors , a large British dealership. Amazon said customers would be able to explore financing options before reserving a car and completing the purchase in physical dealerships. More brands and dealers will be announced before the launch of the UK service.

Amazon will go up against online new and used dealers, as well as traditional physical dealerships. Car companies also sell directly to consumers through their websites.

The share price of Autotrader , the UK’s largest car sales website and a member of the FTSE 100, fell 2% on Wednesday after news of Amazon’s move.

Vertu’s share price rose 4% although it also announced acquisitions of dealerships. The company, listed on London’s Alternative Investment Market, was valued at £269m before the announcement.

Back in the financial markets, Wall Street is extending its losses in pre-market trading.

Futures tracking the S&P 500 share index are down almost 2%, while the tech-focused Nasdaq futures are down 3%.

Photos: Eurostar disruption

Eurostar cancels London and Paris trains after unannounced strike

Eurostar has cancelled some of its trains between London, Paris and Brussels today due to an “unexpected” strike.

According to the Press Association, Eurostar is locked in annual pay negotiations with a union in France, where no decision has been made and talks are ongoing.

The 7.01am, 8.01am and 12.31pm trains from London St Pancras to Paris Gare du Nord on Wednesday were cancelled because of the industrial action.

Eurostar said on its website:

double quotation mark Due to unexpected industrial action today, we are experiencing cancellations and severe disruption to our trains between London and Paris today. Other routes might be impacted too. We advise you to change your journey for a different date of travel.

Some trains to and from Brussels were expected to be cancelled too. The 5.01pm train from St Pancras to Brussels-Midi was showing as cancelled online. Here is the full list.

A spokesperson said other routes are “not directly affected but may see some knock-on impact”.

double quotation mark We ask customers not to come to the station if their train is cancelled as they will not be able to travel. Discussions are ongoing with the union and the company remains open and willing to engage in constructive dialogue.”

It comes as Londoners prepare for the first of eight planned 24-hour strikes by Tube drivers on Thursday and Friday.

Members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union started their walk-out from noon on Thursday, with delays and cancellations expected across the Tube network.

This charts the energy price cap over the last few years.

January’s 26% jump in energy prices Britain will make things even harder for people who are near the end of their life, the charity Sue Ryder warned in its response to Ofgem lifting the price cap again.

Dr Paul Perkins , the chief medical director at Sue Ryder , a palliative care and bereavement charity, said:

double quotation mark Today’s announcement will no doubt cause concern for many, but for those living with a terminal illness, it can darken the precious time they have left. It may make them anxious and afraid, wondering how they’re going to keep themselves warm and keep their medical equipment going when they should be spending time making memories with loved ones. Many rely on higher levels of heating to stop symptoms worsening, while others depend on vital electrical medical equipment, which in some cases is keeping them alive. All this leaves them with significantly increased costs. Targeted help with energy costs would remove a substantial burden and allow people to make the most of the time they have left, not spending it watching their bank balance. Everyone deserves to live well and with dignity until the very end.

M&G boss urges UK to stem flood of firms leaving London Stock Exchange after Compass exit

The boss of the British investment group M&G has called on the government to “take a stand” against the long line of companies leaving the London Stock Exchange, after the FTSE 100 caterer Compass Group announced plans to switch its primary listing to New York.

Andrea Rossi , chief executive of M&G, said his fund managers would vote against the Compass’s proposed move.

In a letter to the Financial Times , Rossi warned that its decision to switch away from London was a “warning about the health of the UK stock market”.

He wrote that “when one of the largest members of the FTSE 100 concludes that its interests are better served elsewhere, policymakers cannot regard it as an isolated corporate decision.”

double quotation mark The continued departure of major companies from London’s stock market should concern anyone who cares about Britain’s economic future.

‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s

Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”.

Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”.

Dr Joanne Lunn , Waitrose’s head of health and nutrition, said:

double quotation mark GLP-1s are reshaping the entire food and drink landscape, even for people who aren’t on the medication. As appetite patterns change, customers’ baskets are shifting towards smaller portions, nutrient density and high-satiety (feeling full) foods.

EasyJet boss says can't rule out further job cuts

In other news this morning, the boss of EasyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts at the airline, after a spike in fuel prices this year triggered a collapse in profits.

The airline’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ended in September, compared with £658m in the prior year.

EasyJet, which has agreed to a £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity firm Apollo , warned earlier this year that it had lost more money than expected during the spring, as war in the Middle East pushed up fuel prices and hit travel demand.

Chief executive Kenton Jarvis said the year was “challenging for airlines due to the Middle East conflict and its effect on demand and fuel prices, which materially impacted our financial performance.”

The airline’s fuel bill alone rose by 11% – or £244m – to £2.5bn this year.

Jarvis declined to rule out further job cuts, after it emerged this month that the airline was consulting on cutting up to 50 roles at its head office in Luton. It employs about 16,000 people around the world.

“We continue to look for ways to be more efficient” in the head office, he said, adding that he had “no plans” for cuts to frontline staff such as cabin crew and pilots.

He added that weaker airlines in Europe could face an existential threat from elevated fuel prices.

double quotation mark There could be airline failures, it would not surprise me,” he said. “This will put a lot of pressure on airlines because the fuel increase is still stubbornly high and not all airlines are hedged. We could see some consolidation both from the flag carriers continuing on their acquisition trail, but also potentially with some market failures.

Surging fuel bills have pushed several airlines to collapse this year, such as Spirit Airlines in the US.

Many airlines have already reduced their flight schedules this winter to offset higher bills. This week, Virgin Atlantic boss Corneel Koster said the airline would fly less than planned by “probably about 8% because of the cost of fuel” and “because of the drop in demand in the winter schedule”.

EasyJet also said that it would retire its older, less efficient plans earlier, which it predicted could make about £250m of cost savings.

stories.body:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change , which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN ), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation ) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration ( issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.

stories.body:
South Africa’s local government elections in November 2026 drew attention to the role of mayors in municipal government, particularly in Johannesburg. However, Johannesburg’s mayoralty has a long history, with more than 100 mayors having occupied the chair. Christopher McMichael and Philip Harrison have just published a book, Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City . Harrison answers questions about it.

You wrote the book amid a deepening governance crisis. How does the book speak to this?

The book doesn’t try to solve – or even dissect – the current crisis . Instead, it steps back to view Johannesburg and its governance through the long lens of history.

Cities swing between growth, crisis and stagnation; a single snapshot never tells the whole story. We think history offers hope: circumstances shift.

Taking the long view matters for another reason too. Cities are the product of a complex layering of multiple processes with different time horizons. Johannesburg’s crumbling infrastructure is a prime example. While the past decade’s unstable coalitions have accelerated the decay, essential assets like water, power and road infrastructure are built to last 30 years or more – meaning their current state reflects decades of neglect.

Understanding history transforms how we experience the present.

What were the good years, and what were the bad?

One group’s golden age may be another’s darkest hour. This was, for example, the case in the 1950s and 1960s when the white middle class was realising the benefits of an American-type suburban lifestyle while the Black residents of townships were experiencing heightened state repression.

Nevertheless, some periods are associated with narratives of progress, and others with crisis or stagnation. The optimism in the late 1930s is a case in point.

The Great Depression was followed by a mining boom, with the central business district going high-rise, and new infrastructure laid out across the city. Johannesburg celebrated its golden jubilee in 1936 with the Empire Exhibition , cementing its status as a new and prosperous City of Empire.

Another period of optimism, for white Johannesburg at least, was the early 1970s. The United Party-controlled city council declared an era of civic progress with the construction of a vast network of motorways, the opening of the Carlton Centre as Africa’s tallest building, and a grand new civic centre.

The celebratory mood, of course, ended when the youth in Soweto rose in revolt in June 1976 .

Other moments of hope came in the early 1990s, as the political impasse of the previous decade ended, although the transition was turbulent. The 2000s saw at least a decade of rapid economic growth, though governance controversies persisted.

But there were certainly bad times: the South African War (1899-1902); a bitter struggle between white capital and white labour which culminated in the Rand Rebellion ; two world wars, the influenza pandemic, the Great Depression, and the shock of the Afrikaner nationalist victory of 1948.

The 1980s may have been the city’s low point. A conservative coalition of the National Party and the Independent Ratepayers Association resisted desegregation. It planned to celebrate Johannesburg’s centenary in 1986, but the then president, P.W. Botha, declared a nationwide state of emergency .

The transition in the 1990s was a roller coaster, ending with a financial crisis that nearly bankrupted the city. Over the past ten years or so, the city has seen unstable coalition governments, deteriorated service delivery, and increasing corruption, along with the COVID-19 pandemic and a stagnant economy.

It is a complex story of hope and despair, driven by an entanglement of local and national factors, but it does suggest a city of some resilience.

Why does the mayor matter in all of this?

In the colonial and apartheid years, mayors were ceremonial, elected for single-year terms, with governing left mainly to council committees. Mayors generally acted as a stabilising force, mediating in back rooms between competing interests.

From 2000, with the introduction of the executive mayoralty , mayors mattered far more directly. They led the executive branch and could drive a vision for the city.

From 2019, mayors had to cede power to coalition partners to remain in office. The city administration became a patchwork of fiefdoms.

Mayors, whether ceremonial or executive, make the complexity of city governance visible to the public. However, the mayor is only one of many actors in city administration. Bureaucrats, councillors, union heads and many others play crucial roles.

While we have used the mayor as a lens into city administration, we recognise its limitations. The book tries to contextualise the work of mayors within a much wider landscape of change.

Were there good mayors, and what measures define success?

Good and “bad” are subjective concepts. But we do have a definition of “good” for the colonial and apartheid eras, and for the post-apartheid period.

Before 1994, a “good mayor” was one who pushed the bounds of convention towards a fairer society. White Joburg society was quite conservative overall, and a radically progressive politician was unlikely to become mayor. Nevertheless, there were individuals who tried in their limited ways: Edwin Orlando Leake, who was concerned with housing opportunities for African people; Maurice Freeman, who defended Indian people from discriminatory legislation; Max Goodman, who defied police orders in engaging with protestors; Alec Jaffe, who tried to protect vulnerable tenants from unscrupulous landlords; Monty Sklaar, who promoted multi-racialism in council events.

The most consequential “good mayor” may have been Johannesburg’s first woman mayor, Jessie McPherson, elected in 1945 and representing the Labour Party. She clashed with segregationists and was subjected to a travel ban by the national government for 15 years.

The good mayors were outnumbered by the bad ones, who entrenched civic exclusion and local prejudice.

This leaves us to ask what a good mayor may be in the post-apartheid period; perhaps one who put the promise of making citizens’ lives better into effect.

The first black mayor, Isaac Mogase, served during the transitional period of the 1990s, and with his integrity and steady demeanour, provided confidence in local government. Amos Masondo, the first executive mayor of metropolitan Johannesburg, benefited from ten years of office, but his discipline, sense of duty and consistent administrative action, even if humdrum at times, was revealed in visible implementation. The transformation of Soweto during his mayoralty was a case in point. Parks Tau introduced progressive city policies, but implementation was limited as he lost the election to Herman Mashaba after five years.

Mashaba, in turn, promised to turn the city into a construction site within 12 to 18 months , but he underestimated the political and technical requirements for achieving this. After Mashaba, a quick succession of eight mayoralties followed (excluding one declared illegal by the high courts).

Based on your sweep of the city’s history, what takeaways do you offer?

We don’t offer explicit takeaways. But we can draw a few suggestions from our work.

One concerns the mayoral system itself. The indirectly elected executive mayor was quite successful in the first 15 or so years of post-apartheid rule. But not anymore.

Because of the instability created by coalition governance, the mayoralty needs a rethink. There are at least two options here.

The first would be to adopt a system of directly elected executive mayors, separating the mayor from the chaos of coalition politics.

Alternatively, some form of non-executive mayoralty could be considered. The mayor would be enjoined to remain above party politics and be a unifying figure.

Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City was published by Jacana Press .

stories.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
stories.summary: The post Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: An illustration shows the silhouettes of a woman speaking at a lectern near a ribbon and housing development, and a man looking at a clipboard while standing next to shovels and construction machinery. In the background are trees and mountains.
stories.body:
Records show that Andrea Bell was personally involved in discussions about state funding of a large apartment project that would pay her husband’s employer $2 million if built. Project backers want $17.5 million from Bell’s agency.

Co-published with Oregon Public Broadcasting and The Oregonian/OregonLive

When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning .

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.

Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.

Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.

Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.

“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.

“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.

Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.

Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.

Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.

Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.

Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”

“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”

A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.

A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”

“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.

Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.

Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.

Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.

stories.summary: The post An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A chart showing an increase in the rate of deaths after an ectopic pregnancy, normalized by the number of live births. In the three-year period starting in 2014, the rate is a little above 4 deaths per million live births. The rate rises sharply for the 2020 to 2022 period and continues to increase,
stories.body:
Our analysis of death certificate data kept by the federal government found ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled, and it’s worse in states with abortion bans. How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?

For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.

For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.

Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level . We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.

This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.

A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.

How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?

The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.

It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.

“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.

“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”

Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013.

The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.

This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.

We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.

It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.

Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.

This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.

Read More

We asked several experts why death rates were going up, but there was no consensus. And while our analysis can’t establish whether there is a causal link between abortion bans and the worse outcomes in the states that have them, there is no evidence that officials are stepping up to examine this question or offer solutions. Even professional organizations, such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, have yet to provide specific guidance to doctors about how to adequately treat women with suspected ectopic pregnancies in states with abortion bans.

But experts say the trend we uncovered is unacceptable and requires a response. As Courtney Schreiber, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology, told us, our work “raises concern that young women are dying from a preventable cause at an increasing rate. That is not what we should be seeing in the United States of America.”

We hope you’ll read our recent investigation , which includes more details on potential explanations for this trend and stories from women in states with abortion bans who faced delays in care. We plan to continue reporting on maternal health and the impact of abortion bans for the foreseeable future.

stories.title: Two Banks, Two Reckonings: What Paraguay and Brazil Share
stories.summary: Corruption plagues Latin America's right-wing politicos. The post Two Banks, Two Reckonings: What Paraguay and Brazil Share appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Paraguay's President Santiago Pena pose for a photo during a world leaders' summit on ending the Gaza war on October 13, 2025 in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt. (Suzanne Plunkett - Pool / Getty Images)

Earlier this month, Paraguay’s Senate removed President Santiago Peña. All 44 senators present voted to oust him over the collapse of a digital bank that froze the accounts of nearly half the population, a day after the lower house impeached him unanimously. He was placed under house arrest that evening, and the next day a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility. He is charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain; on November 13, prosecutors added a criminal association charge , accusing him of leading a scheme with five former central bank directors to shield Ueno from scrutiny . Peña denies wrongdoing, and his lawyer says that he will plead not guilty.

The bank was Ueno. It had about three million customers , roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adults, and held more than $800 million in public funds, including about $380 million from the state pension and health fund. Regulators moved in after its solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum. Peña remained a business partner of the conglomerate that owns Ueno until March 2025, though the bank says he was never a shareholder. Prosecutors allege that, as president, he pushed state entities to deposit public money in Ueno despite concerns about its health, and that two Ueno loans of about $500,000 in 2024 helped pay for his mansion. Bank executives have been arrested, and the former central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, who once ran Ueno, is also charged.

This was a second embarrassment for the Latin American far right after the loss of Flavio Bolsonaro in the Brazilian elections at the end of October. Peña was a key ally of Donald Trump. His business-friendly economic model was touted by neoliberal admirers like Argentina’s Javier Milei . Peña and Bolsonaro don’t just share a political affinity. They both have faced similar financial scandals.

Flávio Bolsonaro is currently under investigation for the Banco Master scandal in Brazil’s central bank liquidated Banco Master on November 18, 2025, and the collapse triggered a payout of nearly $7.7 billion from the credit guarantee fund, the largest in its history. The Federal Police’s Operation Compliance Zero has since arrest ed banker Daniel Vorcaro’s father and the former president of the public Banco de Brasília, and Senator Ciro Nogueira has also been a target. Leaked messages show Flavio asking Vorcaro for 134 million reais for a film about his father, Jair Bolsonaro (under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence). The younger Bolsonaro calls the funds he received—approximately half of what he requested—private money for a private movie.

The scandal certainly dominated the presidential campaign, but it did not likely decide the result. Although directly implicated, Flávio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in the first round, casting himself as an outsider at a time when the banking scandal seemingly affected the whole ruling class. A Datafolha poll found Brazilians split on whom the scandal tarnished more: 34 percent said the left, 27 percent the right.

The shared lesson is that a fast-growing bank can sit close to political power while regulators look away. In Paraguay, government deposits in Ueno rose to about 29 percent of its deposits after Peña took office. In Brazil, Banco Master’s license was approved under Jair Bolsonaro’s government, yet the scandal reached justices and politicians across the spectrum.

Both countries also remember what a bank freeze can do. In Brazil, in 1990, President Fernando Collor de Mello froze balances above 50,000 cruzados novos, and the stock market fell more than 20 percent as the state seized savings. Today’s crises come from private banks, and the response has been arrests and impeachment.

Paraguay’s new president, Pedro Alliana, comes from the same political machine. He rose through the Colorado Party faction led by former president Horacio Cartes, whose U.S. sanctions over alleged corruption, which he denies, were lifted last year. Alliana has confirmed holding a certificate of deposit of about $640,000 at Ueno, and the lower house rejected a motion to impeach him. No charges against him have been reported, and holding the deposit does not by itself show involvement. Analyst Andrew Nickson doubts the case will reach the powerful, saying that “only scapegoats are likely to suffer long-term sentences.”

Marc Ostfield, the U.S. ambassador to Paraguay from 2022 to 2025, argues that Ueno’s collapse exposed a political machine built around Cartes and his protégé Peña, in which public deposits and pension money flowed to friendly banks, Ueno and the Cartes-linked Banco Basa, while Washington overlooked the warning signs because Paraguay was a useful ally. Strategic alignment, he says, is not the same thing as democratic resilience. Cartes reportedly backed Peña’s removal, and the new vice president, Antonio Barrios, is another longtime Cartes ally, so the power structure may be largely intact.

The financial picture has also darkened. Central bank president Jorge Schreiner told AFP that losses could reach $1 billion in the worst case. The deposit guarantee fund has advanced roughly $650-700 million to move the accounts of about 1.8 million depositors to other banks, with payouts of up to about $18,000 per person, and Schreiner says that the fund will absorb the first loss. Bonds Ueno issued abroad are not protected by law. Ueno has assets worth $1 billion or more, but valuing them will take one to two months , and an IMF mission is expected in December. Officials said earlier in November that nearly 95 percent of savers had been compensated, yet about $800 million in public money, including pension funds, remains at risk , and the labor minister says that up to 7,000 people lost jobs at companies tied to the bank. Alliana has pledged to recover the pension money, promising that retirees will be paid .

The test is conviction, not arrest. Brazil’s probe has drawn complaints of selective leaks, and Paraguay’s prosecutors were criticized for seeking dismissal of the case against Cartes. Still, in both countries the people who lost access to their money did not stay quiet, and the institutions that were supposed to protect them have started moving. That is the first condition for trust to return.

stories.title: Would Spain Again Say No to the Next Major Attack on Iran?
stories.summary: The right-wing and far-right parties want to make nice with Trump. The post Would Spain Again Say No to the Next Major Attack on Iran? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Secretary-General of the PSOE Pedro Sanchez (left), and the leader of the PP Alberto Nuñez Feijoo (right), during a televised head-to-head debate (Shutterstock)

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez put a direct question to the leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and his principal rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in Spain’s November 19 election debate. Did Feijóo regret his and PP’s No. 2 candidate Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo’s backing for Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran?

Sánchez called the Iran war ‘disastrous,” invoking an equally disastrous precedent in Iraq more than 20 years ago. The question deliberately pointed to a PP government, led by the prime minister José María Aznar, that was one of the key champions of that misbegotten adventure.

Instead of responding directly, Feijóo took a convoluted detour by first claiming that Sanchez was the “only sitting MP who supported a war” by endorsing the Spanish parliament military intervention in Libya in 2011. But the intervention in Libya was backed by 336 members of the Spanish Congress, including those of Feijóo’s PP, several of whom are still in parliament.

Then Feijóo brought up unrelated matters, like the migration crisis in Ceuta earlier this year, before finally answering on the Iran war: “Of course I’m against it.” He then immediately added that Iran was “a dictatorship” and that Hamas and Hezbollah were “delighted” with Sánchez.

Sanchez missed an opportunity to press his rival on whether he would let the United States use the Spanish bases at Rota and Morón for another round of strikes on Iran should such a request come from Washington.

He had solid grounds for insisting on obtaining clear answers.

When the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026, Álvarez de Toledo, Feijóo’s number two, expressed strong support for the operation and urged Spain and Europe to back it unequivocally. Former PP Prime Minister Aznar argued in March that a war to change Iran’s regime was justified. His neoconservative foundation, FAES (Fundación para el Análisis y los Estudios Sociales), still influential in parts of the PP, portrayed Sánchez’s opposition to the war as “ hypocritical and detrimental” to Spain.

Feijóo’s himself argued that Spain should preserve its relationship with Washington and put human rights ahead of international law in his criticism of Sánchez’s response to the war. Curiously, he and his party are considerably less insistent on human rights when it comes to close partners of the West, such as Israel or United Arab Emirates.

What Madrid would do in the case of another request for action by Washington depends not only on PP’s position but also on how much Feijóo would need the far-right party Vox after the November 29 election. The latest polls show that PP and Vox combined enjoy the support of almost half of the voters, while only around 40 percent favor the left bloc. The situation is in flux but the right and the far right could plausibly win an outright parliamentary majority.

Vox leader Santiago Abascal was straightforward in his support for Trump and Netanyahu. In April, he defended the U.S.–Israeli offensive as an exercise in pursuing national interests, while claiming, without citing any evidence, that the Iranian regime has killed 50,000 people and threatens the world with nuclear weapons.

The overlap between parts of PP and Vox has a history. Rafael Bardají, the Aznar adviser who pressed Spain to back the Iraq War, later joined Vox’s leadership team. In March 2026, he offered unconditional support for the U.S.- Israel war and attacked European leaders for failing to join it.

Bardají has spent years advocating for Israel and pressing for a harder line on Iran. He has served as the executive director of the Friends of Israel Initiative , a Madrid-based lobbying group that was launched in 2010 and led by Aznar, and that counts Iran ultra-hawks, such as John Bolton , among its co-founders. Bardaji also cultivated ties with neoconservative groups, like the UK-based Henry Jackson Society and the Washington DC-based Foundation for the Defense of Democracies.

A decision to allow the United States to use the Spanish bases in Rota and Morón or Spanish airspace to attack Iran would not be popular. In a March poll, 68 percent of Spaniards opposed the strikes and 53 percent backed the decision to deny the United States use of the bases for them.

A Feijóo government could reverse that position while continuing to say that it opposes war. A future U.S. request might concern refueling, transit, or logistical support. Madrid could authorize it while framing it as routine cooperation with an ally. This is the position taken by the center-right government in neighboring Portugal, which authorized the U.S. use of its airbase in the Azores islands while avoiding an open endorsement of the war.

The German Marshall Fund, a think-tank focusing on transatlantic relations, predicts that a PP-led government will take a more permissive stance on the use of the bases as part of an effort to repair relations with Washington. Feijóo’s own Atlanticist instincts—along with fear of Trump’s threats , the lingering influence of Aznar’s neoconservatism, and pressure from the ambitious hawks in his own party, such as Álvarez de Toledo and Madrid’s regional president Isabel Ayuso —would also likely push him in that direction. Vox, though more likely to focus its coalition bargaining on concerns like immigration and domestic policy, would reinforce these tendencies.

The choice would matter beyond Spain. Madrid has been one of the few European capitals willing to translate objections to U.S. and Israeli policy into concrete decisions: refusal to cooperate in any shape or form on the U.S. attack on Iran, an arms embargo on Israel, and the diplomatic recognition of Palestine. Reversing even one of those decisions would weaken Spain’s international standing and turn Madrid from a point of resistance to Trump into another European capital submissive to Washington and Tel Aviv.

stories.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Tethered to Fossil Fuels
stories.summary: The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A pile of sulfur at an oil refinery in Cartagena, Spain. Sulfur, a byproduct of refining, is needed to make phosphate fertilizer. Angel Garcia / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ANALYSIS

The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout.

By Fred Pearce • November 24, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India to southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño , the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

A farmer spreads fertilizer on his land in Indian Kashmir. Firdous Nazir / NurPhoto via AP

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.

Cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Amirhosein Khorgooi / AP Photo

Most discussion about the resource implications of the Iran war has concentrated on disruption to the Gulf’s oil and natural gas exports. But the war has also hindered the production of the two most critical fertilizers in the world: nitrogen-based ammonia, which is made in the Gulf using hydrogen extracted from natural gas, and phosphate fertilizer, whose manufacture requires sulfur extracted from hydrocarbon refining. The conflict has cut the amount of nitrogen supplied to farmers by about a quarter but phosphate supplies by 40 percent.

As the war has progressed, the supply of sulfur has continued to shrink. In May, China, the world’s largest exporter of sulfuric acid, banned sales to foreign manufacturers to protect its own fertilizer supplies. Then in August, Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom’s Astrakhan gas processing plant, knocking out 60 percent of Russia’s sulfur production.

With supplies cut and prices up by more than a third, sometimes exceeding $1,000 per metric ton, much of the sulfur that has been available has been snapped up by the mining industry, which can afford the higher prices. The price hike has left phosphate fertilizer producers in a bind. Many have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, cannot pay for the product. Mosaic, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers, more than halved its U.S. production in 2026 and has announced plans to shut one plant for six months starting in December. “Without affordable sulfur,” production superintendent Hector Mier said last month, the company was “forced to curtail production. That means less fertilizer for farmers and less food grown in American farmland.” Saudi and Brazilian plants have also closed.

As less fertilizer is added to soils, says an analyst, there will be an “erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries.”

Brendan Rice, an agribusiness analyst for the Washington, D.C.-based International Food Policy Research Institute, warns that as less phosphate fertilizer is added to soils, there will be “a slow-rolling erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries” stretching through 2027 and beyond.

The first clear signs of the downturn may emerge in the next three months with the harvest of rice in India and Thailand, soy in Brazil, and corn in southern Africa. Amoah says it will “lock in grocery inflation for years.”

What will happen if the Gulf conflict continues to restrict sulfur supplies?

There is no immediate prospect of a revival of sulfur mining. Only two mines remain open: the Osiek Mine in southern Poland and the Kawah Ijen volcano on the Indonesian island of Java, where a few hundred intrepid miners armed with hand tools clamber down into the crater to dig out yellow blocks of elemental sulfur, which they haul to the surface in bamboo baskets. Neither mine could quickly increase production, analysts say. And a widespread reopening of closed mines would be a costly and risky enterprise when Gulf production of cheap sulfur could resume at least as quickly.

A miner gathers sulfur from Kawah Ijen, an active volcano on the Indonesian island of Java. Oscar Espinosa / SOPA Images / LightRocket via Getty Images

There is sulfur stockpiled at a few refineries — notably some 10 million metric tons around tar-sands deposits in the Canadian province of Alberta, some of which is sent to fertilizer manufacturers in Canada and the U.S. But scaling up distribution quickly for the international market would be challenging. “Every tonne must be excavated off the block, trucked to a melting site, melted, formed, and railed to Vancouver for vessel loading,” says Fiona Boyd , a director of London-based Acuity Commodities. “[It’s] a lengthy and expensive process.”

Experts predict that Gulf supplies of sulfur will eventually resume. But that will only postpone the day, says Maslin, when the world faces a long-term sulfur crunch as demand rises while supplies falter.

On the demand side, most observers expect a rapid increase in the use of sulfuric acid as more metals are refined to make batteries. And as the world’s population continues to rise, feeding more people will also likely require more sulfur to make more phosphorus fertilizer. Overall, Maslin sees the market growing by around 60 percent to 400 million metric tons by midcentury.

Farmers could reduce their use of synthetic fertilizers by nourishing their soils with animal manure and farm waste.

But at the same time, he says, supply is set to crash as the world’s energy system decarbonizes, with consumption peaking and then falling sharply over the next three decades, slashing the production of sulfur waste at refineries. In 2022, Maslin and his University College London colleagues calculated that shifting away from fossil fuels “could create a shortfall of sulfuric acid as large as 320 million [metric tons], or 130 percent of present-day production.”

The supply crunch would drive up the cost of sulfur, Maslin said. Then, as now, farmers — and the world’s food supply — would be the likely losers.

To address the shortfall, farmers could reduce their dependence on both nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers by nourishing their soils organically. Animal manure and organic farm wastes are rich in both chemicals. But few agriculturalists expect such methods to do more than moderate rising demand for synthetic fertilizer — and the sulfur needed to make it.

So where will the sulfur come from? We could go back to large-scale mining. Unlike some strategic materials, the world is not short of geological sulfur. It is the 13th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, found in volcanoes, salt domes, and in sedimentary deposits created by the evaporation of seawater.

A tractor spreads fertilizer on a soybean field in Goias, Brazil. Mateus Bonomi / Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

But Maslin warns of the risks. “Direct mining of elemental sulfur is dirty, toxic, [and] destructive.” To minimize the damage, he says, “the world needs to cut demand by recycling and using alternative industrial technologies that avoid intensive use of sulfuric acid.” Widespread commercial recycling of sulfur has potential. Sulfuric acid is a major component of widely used lead-acid batteries, for instance. In the U.S. it is widely recycled along with lead.

Another approach is to cut demand for sulfur’s biggest use — making phosphate fertilizer — by recycling the phosphates found in human sewage, which is where much of the material used to grow our food ends up.

More than half the world’s population is now connected to sewage systems. Sewage sludge from treatment works may contain industrial contaminants but is generally considered safe for application to cropland and often sold or given to farmers in developed countries, notably the U.K. and the U.S. Sludge incinerators in Japan and Germany sell their leftover ash, still rich in phosphates, either to farmers or to fertilizer manufacturers. Willem Schipper, a Dutch consultant in industrial chemistry, calculates that current sewage systems worldwide could deliver around a million metric tons of phosphates each year. That is roughly 3 percent of what is mined each year, but it would trim the need for both sulfur and phosphate, a rock that is itself in increasingly short supply.

By removing phosphates from raw sewage at treatment works, recycling would also reduce the environmental impacts of high levels of phosphates in rivers, where the chemical spurs the growth of plants and algae that block sunlight from penetrating the water and lower oxygen levels. So, while one version of a circular economy might falter as fossil fuels are sidelined, another, smaller circular economy could emerge.
