stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report
stories.summary: Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A coal mine in Jharkhand, India. Vishal Kumar Singh / AFP via Getty Images via Inside Climate News

Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations.

The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice, and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries — Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption — are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 1.5 degree C warming target in the Paris Agreement.

Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment .

The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”

Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.

“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 1.5 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”

“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”

The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.

In particular, the climate, environment, and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.

Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”

Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.

“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

— Bob Berwyn , Inside Climate News

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.summary: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. stories.body:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

T here are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration , Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia , which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along any one human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Peyton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth Social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

China-made lithium-ion batteries, which are relatively low-cost, dominate Ofgem project shortlist

A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears over the risk of foreign interference they could pose to Europe’s energy systems.

Ofgem, Great Britain’s energy regulator, published a provisional shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme in June. The list was dominated by projects relying on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software.

The low cost of lithium-ion batteries meant 11 projects were able to outcompete homegrown renewable energy storage technologies to make Ofgem’s 16-strong shortlist in line for financial support. The energy watchdog is expected to confirm the final projects selected for financial support in the coming weeks.

The shortlisted projects include some backed by developers that routinely rely on Chinese battery makers, one of which was recently the subject of an “ethical hack” by a German cybersecurity company that claimed to have accessed hundreds of thousands of solar installations across Europe.

Ofgem is under pressure to bring forward investment in battery projects that can store renewable energy and release it back to the grid for at least eight – hours at a time to help reduce the cost of balancing the grid.

But senior industry sources have said that the regulator’s assessment criteria for its new battery support scheme have not adequately considered the security and economic benefits of backing British storage technologies over cheaper Chinese imports.

Invinity Energy Systems, a British producer of vanadium flow batteries , threatened to reconsider its plans to manufacture batteries in the UK after Ofgem selected just one project that uses its alternative energy storage technology in its shortlist.

The regulator is expected to finalise the scheme months after a report by Michael Collins, a former deputy head of national security strategy at the UK Cabinet Office, warned that Europe was “sleepwalking” into a series of economic and national security problems because of an overreliance on Chinese-made green technology.

Ofgem’s assessment is heavily weighted towards the cost of each project. Although the regulator considers each project’s proposed IT and security measures, this is based on the extent to which these systems might delay “their stated delivery timelines” in the early 2030s.

The regulator does not appear to specifically consider the risk of security breaches during the lifetime of the projects once they are delivered, although developers would be expected to comply with the government’s general cybersecurity guidance.

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: “We assessed projects against the legal and policy framework set by government and parliament, and are carefully considering consultation responses before reaching final decisions.”

Battery developers Field Energy and Statera Energy, which are behind seven of the lithium-ion projects shortlisted by Ofgem, both have long-established links to Chinese manufacturers which provided the batteries used in past projects.

after newsletter promotion

Field Energy is behind five projects on the shortlist and has typically sourced its battery technology from Envision Energy, one of six companies closely linked to the Chinese Communist party according to US senators.

Statera had three projects shortlisted, including one pumped hydro power project and two lithium-ion batteries, and in the past sourced batteries from Envision, as well as the Chinese solar and battery maker Sungrow. Sungrow was the company targeted in the ethical hack earlier this year.

Both companies said they took security seriously and complied with all national security guidance at their sites. Amit Gudka, the chief executive of Field and the former boss of collapsed energy supplier Bulb , said the company wanted to play a part in creating a UK-based battery manufacturing industry to support future projects.

A UK government spokesperson said: “The security of our energy system is our priority and we are taking action to build secure and resilient battery supply chains and reduce vulnerabilities, while investment in the UK’s energy sector is subject to the highest levels of national security scrutiny.”

stories.body:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.

China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.

The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.

Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged .

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.

The hashtag “Chen Jining under investigation” had amassed about 240m views on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo by Wednesday morning, with many users saying they were “shocked” and “stunned” in comments under state media posts.

“This is arguably the biggest political news to come out of China in a few years,” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School specialising in contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote on X.

Zhang pointed to Chen’s status as a rising political star who had been seen as “a near-lock for the politburo Standing Committee”, China’s highest political decision-making body.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign , which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged , including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.

“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ‘self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.

“If anything, it continues to intensify.”

The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.

Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

“Chen Jining is no ordinary fallen official … [He is] an exemplar of someone who rose from the specialised field of environmental protection to the pinnacle of political power,” Mao Shoulong, a professor of public administration and policy at Renmin University of China, wrote in a commentary on WeChat.

“His downfall, therefore, is not merely that of an individual, but of an entire type of official, a model of political advancement, and a set of assumptions about the relationship between technology and politics, expertise and power, and competence and loyalty,” Mao wrote.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.

stories.body:
Several members of chat set up after alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they had been contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.

Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the next day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company .

The group’s chat history, seen by Guardian Australia, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group that they or their parents had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the next day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.

Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.

HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police in China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.

More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC .

Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she had received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.

Wang said the police seemed unaware that the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, she said they had threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China.

“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China,’” Wang said.

Jack (not his real name), who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he had joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He had received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, the global spokesperson for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.

Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.

She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found that the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou , and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously said that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

after newsletter promotion

WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes about wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.

“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. But these workers were usually working for projects controlled by China’s state companies.

Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”

The opposition home affairs spokesperson, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.

The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.

The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

stories.title: None of UK government's £2.5bn steel package spent in Wales, figures show
stories.summary: Wales is home to the UK's largest steelworks which is currently transitioning to an electric arc furnace.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at Port Talbot by the end of 2027

Published 24 November 2026

Wales has not received any money from the UK government's £2.5bn steel industry investment plan announced in February 2025, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request.

The UK's Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade confirmed that "the government has not spent, nor allocated, nor committed any money under the £2.5bn commitment in Wales".

The FOI was obtained by the Liberal Democrats, whose Welsh leader David Chadwick said that Welsh Labour MPs needed to "demand a fair share for Welsh steel now, before their own government spends the rest".

The UK government said it had "invested extensively to secure steelmaking" in Port Talbot.

The department's FOI response noted that £751m had been invested in the nationalised British Steel site in Scunthorpe and another £172m spent stepping in to save Specialist Steel UK in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands.

Wales is home to Port Talbot's Tata Steel site, the largest steelworks in the UK, which closed its last blast furnace in September 2024 .

A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at the site by the end of 2027, but there are concerns it could now be delayed due to grid connection issues .

Speaking on 24 February 2025, following the announcement of the new steel investment plan, the then-Labour energy minister Sarah Jones said the £2.5bn "could benefit regions across the UK - like Scunthorpe, Rotherham, Redcar, Yorkshire and Port Talbot - which have a strong history of steel production".

She added the money would be "spent on initiatives that would give the industry a long future - such as supporting the transition to electric arc furnaces or other improvements in UK capabilities".

As of October, the UK government had spent £751m on sustaining British Steel in Scunthorpe, since ministers took it into full public ownership in July 2025.

But the National Audit Office warned in March that spending on the site could exceed £1.5bn by 2028 , external .

The £172m spent on Specialist Steel UK has funded things such as ongoing site safety and wages, since the company entered liquidation in August 2026.

In September the UK government announced plans to nationalise the business , which has sites in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands.

In September 2024, Tata Steel in Port Talbot was promised a £500m subsidy from the UK government towards a new electric arc furnace, alongside a commitment by Tata Steel to invest £700m of its own money .

That investment was a conditional grant, not part of the £2.5bn steel industry investment fund announced in 2025.

Port Talbot is home to the largest steelworks in the UK

In March 2026 Plaid Cymru MP Ben Lake asked how much of the £2.5bn steel industry fund would be spent in Wales, to which the then-minister in the Department for Business and Trade, Chris McDonald, said the Welsh secretary would have a role in attracting investment for Welsh steel projects.

"The National Wealth Fund will be the UK government's main mechanism for providing financing for investment in the steel sector.

"Investment decisions are made by the National Wealth Fund on a case-by-case basis and it supports promising projects across the United Kingdom," he said.

"Specifically for Wales, the Secretary of State for Wales will convene the National Wealth Fund and the private sector in a new initiative to help attract investment to Welsh steel projects, to support communities across Wales that rely on the industry."

Chadwick said the lack of investment into Wales from the plan was "the latest in a long line of Labour betrayals of Wales".

"Labour was happy to talk about saving Welsh steel when it wanted Welsh votes," he said. "Now we know what those promises were worth.

"They'll put Wales in the press release, pose in a hard hat in Port Talbot and tell us how much they care. Yet, so far, they haven't delivered a single penny to Wales from their much-lauded steel fund."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham was asked by Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey in Prime Ministers Questions "why on Earth" no money had been spent in Wales and whether Burnham would meet him and Chadwick "to put right this latest betrayal of Welsh industry and jobs"?

Burnham said there was "more to be done" on supporting Port Talbot's steel industry.

He added: "On the steel industry and particularly in Wales... the government has invested heavily in Tata steel in Port Talbot in the electric arc furnace .

"We have as a government invested heavily in steel transition in south Wales".

A UK government spokesperson said it had "invested extensively to secure steelmaking in Port Talbot, in local jobs and in the future of the town.

"This includes £500m to support the £1.25bn transformation of Tata Steel Port Talbot into a modern electric arc steelworks, £102m direct government support for workers and businesses affected by Tata's transition, £64m towards upgrading the port and £14.8m into town centre regeneration.

The spokesperson added the government had also committed to invest up to £2.5bn rebuilding the UK steel industry, including through the National Wealth Fund, "which welcomes applications that meet its criteria from companies in Wales and across the UK, and our steel strategy is also delivering for Welsh steelmakers".

stories.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
stories.summary: The draft proposal could see the UK join the scheme without having to increase import taxes on Chinese cars.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 hours ago

The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by European ambassadors later on Wednesday.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Alignment with higher EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles would increase their price in the UK, at a time when they have become increasingly popular.

It also raises the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on cars made in the UK.

'Real concern'

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times , external , is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. After Wednesday's meeting of EU ambassadors, it will be discussed again by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting before Christmas.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

After last week's EU-UK summit in Brussels, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Made in Europe had become a "source of real concern across the British economy, particularly for our car makers".

"It will come as a relief to workers that the UK and EU committed in Brussels to avoid measures that would harm each other's industries," he added.

State-run Global Times says reports about CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy were ‘malicious’

Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return

Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?

Chinese media have reacted with glee to the dramatic reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, with one commentary warning against future “witch-hunts”.

An article published on Tuesday in the state-run outlet the Global Times said US media reports about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset were “malicious” and “negatively impacted American public perception of China”.

Huang was reinstated to the US artificial intelligence company on Tuesday, weeks after he was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs , including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from Donald Trump.

The Global Times warned that future “political witch-hunts” against companies and individuals accused of links to Chinese intelligence could take the form of investigations and congressional hearings.

“Certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering [sic],” it said.

In another article, the influential blogger Niu Tanqin wrote that Huang’s return indicated that the “so-called female spy allegations are complete nonsense”.

Niu also said that China would be flattered by Donald Trump’s suggestion, made in an interview with CNBC, that Huang could be poached by China.

The US president said on Monday that Xi Jinping, China’s leader, described Huang as a “brilliant man” in their recent meeting in Shenzhen, a city in southern China.

Trump said that, despite the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s affair with the alleged China intelligence asset Alice Huang – no relation – “the bigger threat would be losing the brainpower of somebody like Jensen”.

Nvidia produces the world’s most advanced semiconductors, which underpin the artificial intelligence sector. US export controls have blocked Nvidia from shipping its most sophisticated models to China in a bid to slow down the country’s AI development. Huang has pushed for looser regulations, arguing that it is better to keep China dependent on US technology rather than spur Chinese innovation.

Trump said he had personally intervened with the Nvidia board, which had previously ruled out reinstating Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”

Huang’s comeback caused Nvidia’s shares to soar on Monday, adding almost $1tn (£763bn) in market value to the company, which props up much of the US stock markets.

after newsletter promotion

Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the intelligence committee, said : “I have warned the administration from the start about communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry declined to comment on Huang’s reinstatement. The government has consistently denied the espionage allegations, calling them “slander and defamation”.

Several accounts on Chinese social media shared memes and AI-generated videos showing Huang in various revenge scenarios. In one video, shared by an influential blogger, with more than 1.1 million followers, Huang is reimagined in the Arnold Schwarzenegger movie The Terminator, in the famous “I’ll be back” scene.

In another video, Huang is reimagined as Jack Nicholson’s murderous Jack Torrance in the 1980 horror film The Shining. Huang is shown using an axe to destroy a locked bathroom door, terrorising an AI-generated Colette Kress, who was Nvidia’s interim boss , who is cowering behind it. The video ends with an AI-generated “Here’s Jensen!” channelling Nicholson’s famous line, “Here’s Johnny!”, from the movie.

Analysts believe that the saga also demonstrated to Beijing how power works in the US.

“The lesson Chinese policymakers are likely drawing is neither subtle nor complicated: Donald Trump remains the most influential political figure in America and, in many respects, the most consequential variable in the trajectory of US-China relations,” wrote George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group, a consultancy, in a post on Substack.

stories.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
stories.summary: Some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

The UK government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

Writing in the Guardian, , external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women."

He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse".

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

The Close the Consent Gap campaign is proposing that 16-year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson said there is a question about what is considered "appropriate" for 16 and 17-year-olds.

She said: "I think some of the cases that we've seen where you have a huge age difference and often where you've got a much older adult man, who is in a position of authority, having a relationship with a 16 or 17-year-old makes me feel deeply uncomfortable."

She added: "I think we do need to look at that, but it's complex, we want to look at all of the options and we'll be setting out more and making sure survivors, women's groups and others are involved in that so we can get this right."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Scotland's justice secretary Neil Gray earlier this month said the Scottish government would "consider carefully any evidence-based proposals intended to strengthen protections for young people" when asked about a staggered approach.

He also said there were "no current plans" to change the general position of the age of consent being 16.

A complication with changing the age of consent in Scotland is how it would affect marriage law which allows people to marry or enter a civil partnership at 16. The legal age of marriage in England and Wales is 18.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada , external the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says Published 15 November

Recent high-profile cases including Russell Brand's rape conviction and allegations made against David Walliams have prompted conversations about both the age of consent and NDAs.

Mia Latter, a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, has called for the age of consent to be changed.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Latter said she was "delighted" the government was considering whether to stagger the age of consent, describing it as a "step in the right direction".

In the same week that Brand was convicted, ITV News and the Guardian reported that David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

In late 2023, Walliams' publisher HarperCollins started an internal inquiry about the author's alleged inappropriate behaviour with young female staff.

A female staff member left the company with a pay-out and an NDA.

A spokesperson for the publisher has said: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams.

"We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."

stories.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
stories.summary: Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view. Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.
