stories.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
stories.summary: Claire Waxman tells the BBC Andy Burnham needs to put justice in his 10-year plan for government.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Claire Waxman said the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe

Published 24 November 2026

The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

'Very poor' letters

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme , the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system.

'Broken system'

As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system.

The survey report will argue this would improve coordination between different agencies, as well as allowing victims to monitor when they will access the various legal rights they have under the Victims' Code.

It will also call for an "end-to-end" review of how victims navigate the system, similar to recent reviews that have focused on sentencing or the courts.

Responding to the survey results, Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government was doing "everything we can to fix the broken system we inherited".

She added that ministers had already taken steps to improve the court backlog, and would be publishing an update to the Victims' Code next year.

She said this would be easier for victims to understand, and would set "clear expectations for criminal justice agencies and help victims feel supported".

stories.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
stories.summary: A household using a typical amount of energy would see its annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 November 2026, 00:03 GMT

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.

A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices , paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025.

The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.

Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households.

Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms.

The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest.

People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits.

What is the price cap?

The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means:

For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. The electricity price is often pegged to gas, owing to gas-fired generation.

Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine.

Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system.

It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.

"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.

'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'

Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house.

stories.title: Salon owner's chore woes prompt idea for new app
stories.summary: A salon owner sets up a skill-swapping app after she and clients were "moaning" about chores and admin.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Marie King says TradeOff now has 300 registered users who are exchanging all manner of services

Published 1 hour ago

A salon owner says she was inspired to set up a skill-swapping app after she and her clients spent time "moaning" about chores and admin.

Marie King, who owns Finishing Touches Beauty, in Leckhampton, Cheltenham, set up Trade Off UK after some of her clients expressed concerns they could no longer afford to get their nails done, and so they began exchanging tasks like cooking for beauty treatments.

"I'd be more than happy to spend an extra hour in the salon doing somebody's nails, rather than going home and cooking a lasagne for my kids," she said.

Rebecca O'Meegan, who exchanged skills with King and other app users, said: "It felt good to be useful and it was lovely for it to be reciprocated".

More from Gloucestershire

'Hope' as Black Friday ad ban launches in UK first Published 8 hours ago

'Deep-seated cultural issues' within police force Published 20 hours ago

King said that with the cost-of-living crisis, luxuries, like beauty treatments, were often "the first thing" those finding it difficult would drop.

"I was like, 'Oh, that's a bit of a shame', and then in the next sentence, I'd be saying things like, 'I've got to bake a birthday cake tonight, which I am terrible at'," she said.

"It was just a conversation, and then [the client] said, 'I'll bake the cake for you, and then you do my nails'."

King said the app, which launched in June, now has 300 registered users, with a "community" of people offering everything from catering and baking to PT sessions and dog walking.

Nail technician services are among the skills being offered out to TradeOff users, along with gardening, weeding, sewing, and filling out forms

"A lot of people will say, 'I don't have any skills', and then you start talking to them and then they say about their hobbies," King said, adding things like sewing, gardening and weeding are all skills.

"I'm not very good at sewing, it would take me probably three times the amount of time to actually do it, where if I just gave it to someone, it'd probably take them half an hour.

"You're making valuable time for yourself by giving that job to somebody."

O'Meegan, a former operations manager, said she wanted to help King and offered to do a report for King in exchange for getting her nails done, but it "grew into so much more".

"It was something that came easily to me, I was really happy to help, and then when Marie said, 'I'll exchange it for your nails', which I was having done once a month, it seemed like such an obvious thing to do," O'Meegan said.

"I've dog sat, I've mowed a lawn, and I've offered decluttering services."

However, anyone wanting to take part in such service exchanges are still subject to tax rules, according to HMRC.

King confirmed HMRC's rules still applied to her bartering and exchanging services, even when no money changed hands, but the £1,000 annual trading allowance might apply to individuals.

She also said exchanged skills could be a hobby or an interest and not related to someone's business, which could exempt them.

A HMRC spokesperson said: "Businesses exchanging goods or services may still have income tax, VAT and record-keeping obligations and should check the rules that apply to them on GOV.UK."
